target: AG1’s claim that school dissection mostly uses already-deceased animals and fetal-pig byproducts, so it does not drive wild capture or biodiversity loss
objection: School dissection animal supply is not mainly harmless use of dead byproducts; AG2 says about 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, and that wild-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity.

target: AG1’s broader claim that animal dissection is educationally and ethically justified
objection: Animal dissection is ethically and environmentally harmful because the methods used to supply dissection animals are inhumane and harm ecosystems through wild-capture.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is necessary for biology or medical training
objection: Dissection is not necessary for required education because AP Biology and NGSS do not require it, and no U.S. or Canadian medical schools use animals for physician training.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is needed because alternatives are inferior or unavailable
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations teach anatomy and biology equally well or better than dead animals in dissection-based instruction.

target: AG1’s claim that typical school dissection is based on already-deceased byproducts rather than live capture
objection: AG2 directly rejects that sourcing picture, restating that approximately 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild and therefore dissection supply relies substantially on live wild-capture.

target: AG1’s assumption that appropriate safety and ethical standards are being met in dissection classes
objection: School dissection often involves preserved tissues and chemicals, and classrooms frequently fall short on required safety controls like PPE, ventilation, and waste handling, so at least some dissection classes are unsafe or violate safety standards.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection should be allowed because it can be run safely and ethically
objection: Typical dissection sourcing is inhumane and harmful, so the practice violates required ethical standards even before classroom supervision is considered; therefore the safe/ethical exception does not save it.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection offers unique hands-on, three-dimensional anatomy learning that alternatives cannot match
objection: AP Biology and NGSS do not require animal dissection, and alternatives teach as well or better, so there is no required, unique educational benefit that justifies using animals.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection specimens are mostly already-dead byproducts and thus do not create major harms
objection: AG2 says the typical supply chain still relies on wild-caught animals, so dissection commonly involves inhumane animal treatment and biodiversity harms rather than harmless reuse of byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-deceased byproducts and ethical protocols makes dissection acceptable
objection: If dissection relies on inhumane wild-capture and effective non-animal alternatives exist, then using those specimens still violates humane ethical standards; the practice is not ethically acceptable just because some specimens are byproducts.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s sourcing harms are reduced because most specimens are already-deceased byproducts
objection: AG2 argues that the 99% wild-capture figure means the weak-negation exception is satisfied: dissection still violates required ethical/safety standards because sourcing is inhumane and harmful, not merely byproduct-based.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection remains justified if it is safe, ethical, and uses appropriate specimens
objection: AG2 says the sourcing itself violates required ethical standards, and because the class depends on that sourcing, the dissection class violates required ethical/safety standards regardless of classroom procedure.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection can be justified because it has distinctive learning benefits and mostly uses dead byproducts
objection: Even if dissection has some educational value, the typical sourcing is inhumane wild-capture that harms animals and biodiversity, so the ethical violation defeats the justification.
